ch29.note: The Shanghai Race Club kept a large Western-run racecourse in the heart of the International Settlement (on the ground of today's People's Square). Its betting meetings were among the city's chief social and gambling occasions—a place a man might lose himself in the crowd.

The 'Peace Army' (和平军) was collaborationist Chinese troops raised under the Japanese-sponsored regimes for garrison and police duty in occupied areas—not to be confused with the Nationalists' own underground Loyal and Patriotic Army.

Ruijin, a town in Jiangxi, was the capital of the Communists' 'Chinese Soviet Republic' in the early 1930s, before the encirclement campaigns drove them out on the Long March. To have come from Ruijin marks a man as a Communist of long standing.

Linggu Temple, on the wooded hills east of Nanjing beside the Nationalist revolutionary martyrs' cemetery and Sun Yat-sen's mausoleum. Dai Li was buried there after his death in a 1946 air crash—an honored resting place among the martyrs of the state.

ch29.anchor: breaking the vessel while pelting the rat
ch29.note: The idiom tou shu ji qi (投鼠忌器), 'to throw at the rat but spare the vessel': one holds back from striking an offender for fear of smashing something precious that stands beside him.

Renders fanzuo (反坐), the old Chinese legal principle by which a false accuser is made to suffer the very punishment the person he accused would have received—so that laying a false charge carried the risk of the charge rebounding onto oneself.
